opening.headline: When a problem occurs after updating to a new model version, you learn how to roll back by simply moving one label without modifying the code.
body: Let's consider the case where response errors increased immediately after releasing a new model version v8. If the model version number is directly embedded in the service code, rolling back requires modifying the code, rebuilding, and redeploying it. During this time, the outage continues, and it's uncertain whether the previous version remains intact.

In this class, you will learn how to move aliases—names that refer to model versions—forward (upgrade) or backward (rollback). By examining the code, you will verify how alias references differ from fixed version numbers when called from a call address. You will also review the validate, deploy, and run procedures of Declarative Automation Bundles along with the principle of preserving previous versions. Finally, you will explore a case study comparing rollbacks between services that hardcode version numbers and those that use aliases.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the principles of alias-based promotion and rollback
It can distinguish whether a rollback ends in a single line or whether a redeployment is required by reading the call address and configuration.

screens.title: We uploaded a new model and a problem occurred, but we can't revert it.
screens.lead: First, after the new version deployment, examine the scenario where failures occur. Look in the code snippet of the diagram to identify which part makes rollback difficult.

visual.alt: A scene where the model version number is directly written in the service code and a failure alert is displayed next to it.
labels: Version number is fixed in the code
Increased response errors: shortly after v8 deployment
Need to roll back by modifying code and redeploying?

paragraphs: Shortly after releasing the new model version v8, response errors have been increasing. It is likely that the cause is the new model. The fastest remedy is to roll back to the previous version.

However, the service code directly lists the model version as a number. To roll back, you must change the number in the code, go through review and build processes, and redeploy it. During this entire process, the service remains unavailable. Moreover, it's difficult to confirm whether the previous version is still present.

This course discusses a structure that refers to model versions by name tags rather than numbers. If upgrades and rollbacks can be achieved simply by changing name tags, recovery time significantly improves.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Why is rollback difficult? Is it because the previous version has been deleted, or because the service points to a version? Both of these are confirmed in the lesson.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how long it takes to roll back in our current environment.

screens.title: How long does it take to revert?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Since you're not entering an answer, first recall your environment and then try it.

items.prompt: Is the previous version still in place currently?
items.answer: The first condition for rollback is that there must be a version to revert to. If the previous version is immediately deleted once a new stable version is deployed, recovery options are lost when problems arise. Unity Catalog's registered models do not delete previous versions even when a new version is deployed.

items.prompt: Does the service look for a model by version number or by label name?
items.answer: Version-based services require code modifications every time a version is changed. Name-tag-based services can switch to a new version without altering the code, as long as the version pointed to by the name tag updates. Whether rollback can be completed in a single line depends on this choice.

items.prompt: Can a procedure for rollback be documented?
items.answer: When considering procedures during a failure, the process takes longer. To ensure recovery happens within the same time regardless of who handles it, predefined steps—such as verifying previous versions, moving labels, and confirming implementation—must be established. The final case study in this class demonstrates this procedure.

screens.outro: Now let's go through the code line by line that moves the alias.

screens.title: Promotion and rollback: move nameplates with a single line of code
screens.lead: Read the following code from top to bottom. The right-side explanation describes the purpose of each section and the differences that arise when the reading direction changes.

visual.alt: Diagram showing the movement of the Champion badge from v1 to v2 and back to v1.
labels: Previous version is preserved as is

data.code:
from mlflow import MlflowClient
client = MlflowClient()

client.set_registered_model_alias("prod.ml_team.iris_model", "Champion", 1)
client.set_registered_model_alias("prod.ml_team.iris_model", "Champion", 2)
client.set_registered_model_alias("prod.ml_team.iris_model", "Champion", 1)

model_version_uri = "models:/prod.ml_team.iris_model@Champion"
pinned_uri = "models:/prod.ml_team.iris_model/1"

champion = client.get_model_version_by_alias("prod.ml_team.iris_model", "Champion")

notes.note: Assign the Champion label to version 1 of the registered model prod.ml_team.iris_model. The arguments are in the order of the full model name, alias name, and version number. The alias is a name that can change, and when a Champion is assigned to the currently operating version, workloads are directed to target this alias.
If version 2 is specified in the same call, Champion moves to v2. This is promotion. The code or service configuration remains unchanged; only the label moves.
Rollback means restoring the value to 1 in the same call. This is possible because v1 is preserved. If the previous version has been deleted, then this call becomes meaningless.

The @ suffix of an address refers to an alias reference. After the alias changes, the next execution reads the new version. If a batch inference uses this address, Champion is moved, and the next execution automatically writes the new version.

The number after the slash in the address is the version fixed. Regardless of where you move Champion, this call is always v1. It is precisely this approach that requires you to modify the code when a rollback is necessary.

The deployment procedure queries the version via an alias and then updates the endpoint configuration to serve that version. The endpoint does not automatically change merely by alias migration, so this procedure must be executed together with the alias migration.

screens.outro: Having read about upgrade and rollback at the code level, let's now examine the bundle deployment process and the principles for preserving previous versions.

screens.title: Bundle's validate, deploy, run, and previous version retention
screens.lead: Compare how the promotion procedures differ between the legacy stage approach and the Unity Catalog alias approach by alternately selecting these two states. Pay attention to how the previous version is preserved.

states.label: Legacy stage mode
states.body: The Workspace Model Registry managed model versions by transitioning them through stages—specifically from staging to production, and then to archived. Promotion refers to the transition from staging, and the version currently in production can be identified by the version present in the production stage. This approach is specific to workspace-level registries, and for workspaces using Unity Catalog, it recommends using Unity Catalog's model management approach instead. The model registry is disabled by default in new Unity Catalog workspaces.

states.label: Unity Catalog alias method
states.body: Unity Catalog's registered models retain previous versions even when new versions are created, so recovery is possible simply by restoring the alias. The bundle is configured with `validate`, deployed to the target workspace using `deploy`, and executed using `run`. Deployments are made by changing only the target environment in sequence—development, staging, then production—while keeping the same bundle. A bundle's identity is defined by its name, target, and deployer, and bundles with identical values do not interfere with each other during deployment. Moreover, the fact that the catalog name is `prod` only indicates the environment and governance; it is the alias that specifies which version is receiving production traffic.

screens.outro: Having verified the procedures and preservation principles, let's now walk through an example of directly comparing the rollbacks of the two services.

screens.title: Case Explanation: A service that hardcodes version numbers is difficult to roll back.
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down a step-by-step example comparing the rollbacks of two services. Select the following arrow to follow through and see what happens in Service A and Service B respectively.

visual.alt: Diagram comparing the rollback steps of service A, which hardcodes version numbers, and service B, which uses aliases.

steps.title: Context: Two services use the same model
steps.body: Service A has written the version number directly into the code, like `models:/prod.ml.qa/8`, while Service B uses an alias, like `models:/prod.ml.qa@Champion`. Currently, Champion points to v8, so both services are using the same model.

steps.title: Step 1 Failure Occurred
steps.body: Errors increase in v8, affecting both services. Until now, there has been no difference between them. The difference appears only when rolling back.

steps.title: Step 2: Rollback of Service A
steps.body: It is determined that the `/8` in the call string should be changed to 7. Since the code modification requires review, build, and deployment, the downtime will be extended. During this period, errors continue to affect users.

steps.title: Rollback of Service B, Step 3
steps.body: Read the `@Champion` of the call string and reassign it to alias v7. A single line specifying version 7 to `set_registered_model_alias` is sufficient. Do not modify the service code; starting from the read point, use v7.

steps.title: Step 4 Rollback Pre-Check
steps.body: Before rolling back, let's check three things in sequence: whether an earlier version exists, whether the call is to `@alias` or a /number, and when any existing process or endpoint started reading the new version. Batch inference reads the new version on the next execution, but serving endpoints must update their configuration to start serving the new version.

steps.title: 5-step design conclusion
steps.body: Service codes depend on aliases, and the bundle's `deploy` and `run` procedures are responsible for alias transitions. This ensures that upgrade procedures are consistently repeated. Previous versions are not removed until issues are resolved. Even after a new version becomes stable, it must be retained for a certain period to enable recovery from subsequent failures.

steps.title: Conclusion: Two conditions for rollbacks in releases
steps.body: A rollbackable release satisfies two conditions: the previous version is preserved, and the service is referenced via an alias. If either condition is missing, incident response becomes tied to code deployment.

screens.outro: We have completed the example; now I will summarize the key points and conclude.

screens.title: Key takeaway: moving an alias results in a one-line rollback
screens.lead: Summarize the course content under a single release principle. Begin by reviewing the v8 bug from the first scene.

paragraphs: An alias is a mutable label that points to a specific version of a registered model. By attaching an alias such as Champion to the currently running version, workloads targeting that alias can be promoted or rolled back simply by changing the label. Snowflake provides a similar concept using `ALTER MODEL` to refer to `SET ALIAS`, differing only in terminology.

A rollback requires two conditions. First, the previous version must be preserved. Second, the service must reference the version by alias, not by version number. Whether a rollback completes in one line or whether a redeployment is required is determined by the call address `@alias` and the `/number` notation.

Using the deployment's `validate`, `deploy`, and `run` procedures iteratively to consistently upgrade, and determining which version is currently in operation based on aliases rather than catalog names. The serving endpoint must also execute the procedure to update endpoint configurations separately from alias changes.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: When a problem occurs, the first two things to check are whether the previous version remains and whether the call is an alias or a number.

checks.explain: The alias behind the backslash refers to the version it points to at the time of reading, thus becoming v7; however, the number after the slash locks in the version, so it remains v8 even if the alias is moved.

wrong.0: The description is reversed. The one who uses the number (me) remains fixed, while the one who uses the alias (you) moves accordingly.
wrong.2: alias is interpreted at read time rather than at code redistribution, so (a) starts using v7 from the next execution.
wrong.3: (A) only requires the alias to be moved, while (B) requires the number to be rewritten.

glossary.def: A label whose value may change, pointing to a specific version of a registered model.
This is changing the model to move aliases to the new version for use in operations.
Aliasing back to the previous version recovers the issue.
This is an operational principle that retains previous versions without removing them, even when a new version is deployed, serving as a recovery option.
The bundle processing order proceeds as follows: configuration validation, target workspace deployment, and job execution.

misconceptions.myth: If the catalog name is prod, then the model is in operation.
misconceptions.fact: The catalog name represents only the environment and governance. Which version is handling operational traffic is indicated by the alias.

misconceptions.myth: A rollback always requires re-deploying the code.
misconceptions.fact: If the service is referenced via an alias, only the name tag needs to be moved. Redistribution is necessary only when the version number is hard-coded into the code.

misconceptions.myth: Once the new version is stable, it's cleaner to immediately remove the previous version.
misconceptions.fact: Previous versions serve as recovery mechanisms. They must be retained until the issue is resolved and sufficient time has passed, in order to recover from subsequent failures.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Moving an alias is one line for promotion or rollback.
A rollback requires that the previous version be preserved.
The service should refer to aliases rather than version numbers.
The @alias and /number tagging of the call address determines whether a rollback ends in a single line or whether a redeployment is required.
The entity follows a consistent iteration of validate, deploy, and run procedures to upgrade.
